tiles.cap: Artemis III: four astronauts, two Moon landers, one docking rehearsal in Earth orbit
tiles.nums: planned length of the 2027 Artemis III mission in low Earth orbit
tiles.p1: NASA set out on Friday 23 October how Artemis III will fly. Launching in 2027, it will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas and ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano into low Earth orbit aboard Orion, launched on the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Over a planned 14 days they will rendezvous and dock with test versions of two Moon landers: Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 and SpaceX’s Starship Version 3.
tiles.p2: Why Earth orbit first: everything learned here, says Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons, gets NASA closer to landing on the Moon in 2028, when Artemis astronauts are due to begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole.
deep: The order of events

Blue Origin goes first, launching a Blue Moon Mark 2 test article into a circular low Earth orbit; it can stay up for as long as 30 days, which gives the schedule room. Orion follows and docks, and the astronauts spend about two days inside the Blue Moon test article checking the cabin environment, controls and life-support systems first-hand.
Then Starship
SpaceX launches a Starship Version 3 test article from Florida. Orion will rendezvous and dock with it in a test expected to last up to two hours. The crew will not go inside Starship on this flight.
Spare days

Orion then has up to five more days in orbit for checks of the Orion Crew Survival System suits and docking-sensor tests, a cellular biology experiment, and trials of ways to bring Moon samples back to Earth. Splashdown is in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California.
Three at once

“We’re launching three spacecraft on three different rockets and testing how they operate together,” said Parsons in NASA’s account of the plan. He presented it at a Kennedy briefing on Friday with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya. Artemis IV is planned as the first Artemis mission on the lunar surface.

tiles.cap: 8 pm tonight: two astronauts step outside to bolt a roll-out solar array onto the ISS
tiles.nums: of planned work outside the station, starting 8 a.m. US Eastern, 8 p.m. in Singapore
tiles.p1: Mission managers gave the go on Wednesday. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency set their suits to battery power at 8 a.m. US Eastern time, which is 8 p.m. in Singapore, and that is the official start of the spacewalk. The job: install a new roll-out solar array on the station’s port-side truss, about six hours and 45 minutes of work outside.
tiles.p2: Menon will ride the Canadarm2 robotic arm with the array in hand while Kutryk, tethered to the station, moves along the truss to meet him.
deep: Step by step

First the pair unbolt the roll-out solar array from the temporary stowage platform where it has been kept. Menon carries it to the truss worksite riding the end of Canadarm2. Kutryk translates to the port truss worksite on tethers and helps finish the installation. Then mission controllers on the ground remotely activate the array and it begins generating power.
Who is watching

NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney spent Wednesday familiarising themselves with lighting conditions and camera locations so they can monitor the spacewalkers and operate Canadarm2. NASA+ live coverage starts at 6:30 a.m. Eastern, 6:30 p.m. in Singapore.
Same day, other work

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov uninstalled Earth-photography gear that had been capturing Pacific and Atlantic Ocean landmarks, and flight engineer Anna Kikina tested her fitness in microgravity by jogging on the treadmill in the Zvezda service module.

tiles.cap: Ganymede slid in front of Io on 20 October. That line-up comes round once every six years
tiles.nums: between seasons when Jupiter’s moons can hide one another from Earth
tiles.p1: Ganymede and Io, two of Jupiter’s Galilean moons, met in the sky on 20 October 2026, Ganymede briefly blocking Io from view. Astronomers call it a mutual occultation. NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day for Wednesday 28 October is a video of the meeting by Michael Wong; in it Ganymede is also casting its shadow on Jupiter’s right side.
tiles.p2: Why rare: mutual occultations need Earth’s edge-on view of the moons’ orbits, and that happens only when Jupiter reaches its equinox, once every six years.
deep: Why edge-on matters

For one moon to pass exactly in front of another from our point of view, Earth has to be looking along the plane the moons orbit in. That alignment comes with Jupiter’s equinox, about every six years, so a whole season of these events arrives together and then nothing for years.
Two events in one picture
An occultation is one body hiding another. A shadow is different: at the same time, Ganymede’s shadow was falling on Jupiter, a dark dot on the planet’s disc, so the video shows both at once.
What you would see
The video shows Ganymede moving across and Io disappearing behind it, then returning. It is a rare thing to witness, because the geometry is right so seldom.
tiles.src: NASA APOD, 28 Oct 2026 · video: Michael Wong

tiles.cap: A dead Florida hurricane came back as a bomb cyclone and hit Iceland with 205 km/h gusts
tiles.nums: gust recorded near Eyjafjallajökull volcano in southern Iceland, 14 October
tiles.p1: Hurricane Isaias, the only Atlantic hurricane so far in 2026, made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on 9 October. Its remnants rode the jet stream east across the North Atlantic and developed into a powerful extratropical cyclone. On the afternoon of 14 October the VIIRS instrument on the NOAA-21 satellite caught the spiral brushing past Iceland, where a gust of 205 km/h was recorded near Eyjafjallajökull volcano.
tiles.p2: The storm’s air pressure fell by more than 50 hectopascals in 24 hours, about double the criterion for explosive cyclogenesis, better known as bombogenesis, a bomb cyclone.
deep: What a bomb cyclone is

Meteorologists use the term for a storm whose central pressure plummets. This one fell more than 50 hectopascals in a day, roughly twice the threshold. Some meteorologists think it set a new October low for air pressure in Iceland, after correcting for altitude, likely breaking a record that had stood since 1963.
Numbers from the ground
Sustained winds of 150 km/h on a small island just offshore. Gusts up to 90 km/h in northwestern Scotland the same day, enough to cancel ferries.
How it was seen

The image was captured by VIIRS, the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite, on the NOAA-21 satellite. Earth Observatory published it as Image of the Day on 21 October, with storm clouds in an expanding spiral centred near southern Iceland.
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / NOAA-21 VIIRS

tiles.cap: India’s two docking satellites burned up on the same day, over two different oceans
tiles.nums: circular orbit where SPADEX-A and SPADEX-B started, launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024
tiles.p1: ISRO’s Space Docking Experiment put two satellites, SPADEX-A and SPADEX-B, into a 470 km circular orbit on 30 December 2024 to demonstrate autonomous rendezvous and low-impact docking. Both spacecraft completed every core objective: vertical and radial docking, controlling the docked pair as one (composite control), power transfer between them, undocking and payload operations. ISRO also lists a circumnavigation manoeuvre among the successes.
tiles.p2: On 12 October 2026, with their fuel exhausted, both re-entered: SPADEX-A over the South Pacific around 16:48 UTC, SPADEX-B over the North Atlantic around 23:36 UTC. ISRO posted the account on Friday 23 October.
deep: Why they came down
ISRO says that once the fuel was exhausted in both satellites, their orbits decayed progressively until atmospheric re-entry on 12 October 2026.
The Sun hurried them
Two moderate geomagnetic storms, on 4 and 11 October 2026, accelerated the orbital decay, ISRO says. Space weather, in other words, set the date.
Healthy to the end
Both spacecraft remained healthy until the final telemetry frames were received. Their ends came nearly seven hours apart, each over open ocean: 16:48 UTC and 23:36 UTC.

tiles.cap: Protons in the LHC lap a 27 km ring 11,245 times a second. Check the speed yourself
tiles.nums: laps of the 26,659-metre ring every second
tiles.p1: CERN’s Large Hadron Collider is a ring of superconducting magnets 26,659 metres round, in a tunnel 100 metres underground. Protons go round it 11,245 times a second. Multiply: 11,245 × 26.659 km is about 299,800 km every second. The speed of light is 299,792 km/s. The protons are travelling a hair under it.
tiles.p2: Why so cold: the magnets run at 1.9 K, about −271 °C, colder than outer space, and inside the beam pipes the pressure is ten million million times lower than air at sea level.
deep: The beam

Each beam is structured in around 2,500 bunches, each bunch holding about 100 billion protons, usually spaced 25 nanoseconds apart. The two beams are made to collide at four points around the ring, at 13.6 TeV, the highest collision energy ever reached in a laboratory.
The magnets

1,232 dipole magnets, each 15 metres long, bend the beam; 392 quadrupoles, 5 to 7 metres each, focus it. Eight superconducting cavities per beam, each delivering 2 megavolts at 400 MHz, do the accelerating.
Try the arithmetic

One lap is 26.659 km and there are 11,245 laps a second. How far does a proton travel in one hour of running? About a billion kilometres. And how much of a lap fits in the 25 nanoseconds between bunches? Less than a thousandth.
Right now
The LHC first started up on 10 September 2008. It is due to be shut down from July 2026 for a long upgrade, so 13.6 TeV is the record so far.
tiles.src: CERN, Facts and figures about the LHC

tiles.cap: 1% more electrons than protons: you could push a friend away with the weight of the Earth
tiles.nums: roughly how many times stronger the electric force is than gravity: Feynman’s billion-billion-billion-billion
tiles.p1: Feynman opens his electromagnetism lectures with a thought you can hold in your head. Imagine a force like gravity, falling off with the square of the distance, but about a billion-billion-billion-billion times stronger, with one difference: like kinds repel and unlike kinds attract. That is the electric force. Every atom in you carries it, positive protons and negative electrons, balanced so perfectly that when you stand near someone else you feel no force at all.
tiles.p2: The thought to test: if you stood at arm’s length from someone and each of you had just one per cent more electrons than protons, the repulsion would lift not the Empire State Building, not Mount Everest, but a weight equal to that of the entire Earth.
deep: Why you never notice
Matter is balanced so exactly, Feynman says, that standing near another person you feel nothing. If there were even a little bit of imbalance, you would know it.
The number
A billion is 10⁹; four of them multiplied together make 10³⁶. For two electrons Feynman gives a sharper figure: electrical repulsion over gravitational attraction is 4.17 × 10⁴².
A puzzle he leaves open

Where could such a tremendous number come from? Feynman notes that the time light takes to cross a proton, 10⁻²⁴ seconds, compared with the age of the universe (he used 2 × 10¹⁰ years) gives 10⁻⁴², and wonders whether that is a coincidence. He says the subject is not completely closed.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II ch. 1 and Vol. I ch. 7

tiles.cap: There is a hole in your vision right now. Use this tile to find it
tiles.nums: light receptors in the spot where the optic nerve leaves your retina
tiles.p1: The picture on this tile has a dot on the left and a cross on the right. Hold the screen at about arm’s length. Cover your right eye and look straight at the cross with your left eye; you can still see the dot off to the side. Keep your eye fixed on the cross and bring the screen slowly toward your face. At one distance the dot vanishes. Keep coming and it reappears.
tiles.p2: Swap: cover your left eye, look at the dot with your right, and now the cross disappears instead.
deep: What is going on

The optic nerve, a bundle of nerve fibres carrying messages from your eye to your brain, passes through one spot on the retina, the light-sensitive lining at the back of the eye. In that spot the retina has no light receptors. When the dot’s light falls there, you cannot see the dot.
Why you never notice

Your brain fills in the blind spot with a simple extrapolation of the image around it. Draw a straight line through a dot and a cross on paper: when the dot vanishes, the line looks continuous, with no gap where the dot was.
Measure it

Exploratorium’s model treats the eye as a pinhole camera with the pupil 2 cm from the retina. If the blind spot measures d across on a card held at distance D, its size s on the retina follows s/2 = d/D. Example: a 2.5 cm gap on a card 25 cm away means a blind spot about 2 mm across on your retina.

tiles.cap: A telescope the size of a lunchbox that stacks its own galaxy photos. 840 g, US$419
tiles.nums: pixel size on the Dwarf Mini’s Sony IMX662 sensor, 1/2.8-inch format
tiles.p1: Dwarflab’s Dwarf Mini is in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 special mentions as a lunchbox-sized smart telescope for beginner astrophotographers. Inside: a Sony IMX662 sensor in the 1/2.8-inch format with 2.9-micrometre pixels, shooting 2-megapixel RAW frames. The whole thing weighs 840 g. The lens barrel rotates 225 degrees and the gimbal turns a full 360, so it can find and follow a target picked from the Sky Atlas in its app.
tiles.p2: The trick is stacking: it takes many frames and adds them up on the device itself, so faint nebulae build up without a computer.
deep: The engineering

An equatorial-mount mode allows single exposures of 90 seconds. Three filters: an Astro filter passing 430–690 nm to boost nebula contrast, a dual narrowband filter tuned to hydrogen-alpha at 656.3 nm and oxygen-III at 500.7 nm to cut moonlight and city glow, and a dark-frame filter that auto-captures darks to suppress thermal noise. Dark, bias and flat calibration frames and a Multi-night Super Stack are handled in software.
What the reviewer found

Tom’s Guide’s John Velasco used one for nearly two months and watched the Orion Nebula take form in under five minutes. His caveat: depending on the target, a good result can take anywhere from minutes to hours, and some objects take much longer before details are exposed. His review price was $399; the official page now says $419.
What the spec sheet leaves out
Dwarflab’s page lists no focal length, no aperture, no battery figure and no dimensions. The tripod ($89) and bag ($39) are extra.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 · Dwarflab spec page · Tom’s Guide, 8 Mar 2026

tiles.cap: Earbuds that rewind 30 seconds and save what you just heard. Reviewers asked: is that OK?
tiles.nums: driver in each Nothing Ear (3a) earbud; 4.53 g a bud
tiles.p1: Nothing’s Ear (3a), US$99 / £99, is on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list largely for one feature: squeeze both earbuds and they take an audio snapshot, and you can adjust the window so it includes audio played up to 30 seconds before you squeezed. Inside each 4.53 g bud is a 12 mm driver, Bluetooth 6.0 with the LDAC hi-res codec, active noise cancellation rated up to 45 dB, and an IP54 rating against dust and splashes.
tiles.p2: TechRadar’s Becky Scarrott scored it 4 out of 5 and liked the sound. Her worry is a bud that records calls with only a brief beep as warning: “We need to talk about Call Recording.”
deep: The numbers

Battery: up to 6 hours with noise cancelling off, 4.5 with it on; 25 or 18 hours with the case. USB-C charging, no wireless charging. Frequency range quoted at 20 Hz to 40 kHz. Recordings are stored on the buds themselves, up to two hours.
What reviewers found wrong

Battery life has taken a hit compared with the previous model, the review says; the default sound is overly bassy and a tad quiet; still no wireless charging or hearing tests. The recording features felt like a step too far: “I’m not wholly OK with it.”
The ethics inside the hardware

On an ordinary phone call the other person hears a beep, and muting your microphone does not stop it; on Google Meet a voice announces “This call will be recorded in 3, 2, 1.” The buds cannot capture conversations around you or your own voice, the review notes; what they save is the call or the audio playing through them.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 · nothing.tech · TechRadar, 25 Jul 2026

tiles.cap: Europe is banning the chemical that sets gel nails and 3D prints. NTU built a safer one
tiles.nums: how far a skin adhesive made with the new compound stretches without damaging the skin beneath
tiles.p1: Photoinitiators are the molecules that make a liquid resin turn solid in seconds when light hits it, kick-starting a reaction called polymerisation. Two of the most used, TPO and BAPO, have been identified as reproductive toxins and are being banned in some regions, including the European Union, which has disrupted the gel-nail sector. A team at NTU led by Associate Professor Terry Steele has made a new family of them, aryl diazirines, that are non-toxic; several are soluble in water and liquid at room temperature.
tiles.p2: First published online in NPG Asia Materials on 16 October 2026; NTU announced it on Friday 23 October. The new compounds release nitrogen gas as they cure.
deep: What they showed

Demonstrations included a stretchy skin bioadhesive that extends to more than three and a half times its length without damaging the underlying skin, 3D-printed microfluidic channels from a soybean-oil-based resin, and a gasket cured in place with a handheld UV light to make a water-tight seal.
Why it matters

The most effective and widely used photoinitiators are being regulated out of existence because of toxicity, the NTU release says. Steele: the goal was an activator that is not only safe and biocompatible but also improves on the performance of existing materials.
Next
Lead author and PhD student Naziruddin Ali says the next step is to bridge the gap between the laboratory findings and industrial-scale manufacturing.
tiles.src: NTU Singapore, 23 Oct 2026 · NPG Asia Materials

tiles.cap: Half a metre tall, 2.2 kg, yellow tentacles from dead roots: D. rex, king of the sac fungi
tiles.nums: height of the biggest Dianjunus rex mushrooms; up to 2.2 kg each
tiles.p1: In 2024, researchers surveying fungi in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province, southwestern China, were tipped off by local farmers about something odd: yellowish, tentacle- and spatula-shaped mushrooms growing from decaying tree roots, some reaching 50 centimetres tall and weighing up to 2.2 kilograms. Named Dianjunus rex, they are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies known among all sac fungi, the group that includes morels, truffles and moulds.
tiles.p2: The farmers wanted to know whether it was edible. The scientists’ answer was a new genus, and probably a whole new family.
deep: A giant among small relatives

DNA places D. rex near candlesnuff fungus and dead man’s fingers, whose fruiting bodies are only a few centimetres tall. Sac fungi make their spores in microscopic bladder-like structures and mostly stay small; this one did not.
After the asteroid

The genetic analysis suggests the family first evolved after the mass extinction some 65 million years ago that wiped out the dinosaurs. Indunil Chinthani Senanayake of the Kunming Institute of Botany suggests that in the dark, cold years after the impact, fungi that decompose dead matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesisers.
The name

Rex is Latin for king; Dian was an ancient kingdom of the region. Torda Varga of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, who was not involved, finds it remarkable that a fungus with so enormous a fruiting body went undocumented until now, and suggests environmental DNA databases may hold more relatives. Reported in Frontiers in Fungal Biology.
tiles.src: Science News, 27 Oct 2026 · Song et al., Frontiers in Fungal Biology 2026

tiles.cap: 652 injuries in 1.7 billion rides: the numbers and physics of roller coasters
tiles.nums: the recommended acceleration limit in roller coaster standards, based on research from the space race
tiles.p1: North American parks that chose to share data reported 652 roller coaster injuries in 2024, against about 1.7 billion amusement-park rides a year. That is roughly one injury per 2.6 million rides. Yet Science News reports a fresh debate: the industry standards recommend a 6 g limit on acceleration, based on NASA research from the space race, but disregard any force lasting less than 200 milliseconds, however intense.
tiles.p2: The missing quantity is jerk, how fast acceleration changes. Hit an imperfection in the track and, says mechanical engineer Jurnan Schilder, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.”
deep: History in g

The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City in 1895 and put riders through an estimated 7.5 g, some say closer to 12 g, straining backs and necks. X2 at Magic Mountain in California, the first fourth-dimension coaster with seats that rotate on their own, opened in 2002: 60 metres high, 122 km/h. On 29 September Six Flags announced it would close permanently.
What the research says

A 2002 mathematical model using g-force data from three coasters found accelerations below the levels predicted to cause head injury. A 2017 paper found peak brain effects comparable with mild sports impacts, such as heading a football, and warned that limiting g-forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion.
Jerk and snap

David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, says riders need time to sense acceleration changes. On a fourth-dimension coaster two sets of tracks mean double the variations: “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking,” says Schilder, of the University of Twente in the Netherlands.
Do the division
1,700,000,000 ÷ 652 is about 2.6 million. Then ask what the figure leaves out: only parks that chose to share data are counted.

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer gives you: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not ban AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, giving up at the first sign of difficulty, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and in in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters
These systems invent citations, facts and code that look perfect. MIT’s rule for research: a human verifies, and AI is never listed as a co-author.
Keep it human
The report pushes a regular in-person social component, office hours and project-based work, and says deliberately AI-free experiences have value in themselves.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026

tiles.cap: 864 solar cells on a 6-metre sunshade: NASA’s asteroid hunter is nearly built
tiles.nums: solar cells on NEO Surveyor’s sunshade, together making up to 2 kilowatts, the spacecraft’s only power
tiles.p1: NEO Surveyor is the first spacecraft NASA has built specifically to find large numbers of potentially hazardous asteroids and comets. Its sunshade, built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, stands 6 metres tall and 2.4 metres wide at the base: two flat panels joined at an angle of 23.5 degrees. Its main job is to block the Sun’s glare and keep the telescope cool; it also carries 864 solar cells, the spacecraft’s only source of power, which charge the batteries on board.
tiles.p2: NASA blog update Monday 26 October. Launch is no earlier than September 2027. Dark asteroids reflect little visible light but glow in infrared as the Sun warms them, and infrared is what this telescope sees.
deep: The eye

The telescope’s aperture is 50 cm. Two infrared detector arrays each build a 16-megapixel mosaic of the sky. Seeing an object in two infrared bands lets scientists estimate its temperature, and from that, its size.
Looking where ground telescopes can’t

It will watch for objects approaching from the Sun’s direction and for objects leading or trailing Earth’s orbit, places ground-based telescopes struggle with because of the Sun’s glare. It builds on NASA’s NEOWISE telescope.
The road so far

SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque added the 864 cells in January. Environmental testing finished in March at a thermal vacuum facility in El Segundo, California. In May the sunshade was delivered, ahead of schedule, to BAE Systems in Boulder, Colorado, and inspected in a clean room there in July.
Since then
Coarse Sun sensors, which help the spacecraft work out which way it is pointing, and temperature sensors have been fitted, and the solar array has passed its functional and performance tests.
tiles.credit: Photo: BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems / NASA

tiles.cap: NTU’s 14th satellite is up, carrying the first Singapore-made solar module to fly in orbit
tiles.nums: satellites NTU has launched since X-SAT in 2011; CRIMSON-1 went up on 1 October
tiles.p1: CRIMSON-1 launched on Thursday 1 October on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, on the Transporter-18 rideshare, and was pushed out into low Earth orbit by Exolaunch’s EXOpod Nova deployer. It carries several next-generation perovskite solar cells developed by NTU researchers with Singfilm Solar, an NUS spin-off, including a flexible perovskite module on ultrathin glass, the first Singapore-made solar module flown in orbit. The job: measure how well the cells’ durability and efficiency survive the trip from ground to space, and how much power they make up there.
tiles.p2: NTU news release 2 October. It is one of the first projects backed by the National Space Agency of Singapore under its Space Access Programme.
deep: The other experiment: thinking on board

CRIMSON-1 also carries an edge AI image-processing system. Instead of sending every raw image down a limited radio link, it processes images in orbit and sends less. Researchers will watch how the computer handles heat and power under heavy workloads.
Why perovskites
NTU’s landmark Science paper on perovskite solar cells came out in 2013. The cells are thin and light.
The one before
VELOX-AM, NTU’s 13th satellite, launched in July 2023 and deorbited in August 2026.
Who paid, who helped

Singapore’s government has put S$210 million into the Space Technology Development Programme since 2022. IMDA secured the satellite’s radio spectrum and orbital resources from the ITU; Exolaunch handled launch capacity, mission management, integration and deployment.
